_note: AI-step output. In this prototype the descriptions, formulas and table values were produced by Claude looking at each slide image, standing in for the vision-model step of the pipeline. Everything else (title text, structure, MathML, HTML) is generated by make_accessible.py.

slides.overview: A diagram explaining the nearest neighbour classifier. Five labelled training photos sit on the left, one unlabelled query photo of a cat on the right, and below them a distance metric that compares two images.
parts: Training data with labels: five small photos labelled deer, bird, plane, cat and car.
Query data: a larger photo of a grey tabby cat, marked with a question mark because its label is unknown.
Distance metric: the query cat and the training cat are placed between vertical bars, and an arrow maps the pair to the real numbers.
slides.relationships: The classifier compares the query image with every training image using the distance metric. The training image with the smallest distance gives its label to the query, so here the query would be labelled cat.

math.spoken_context: The distance metric takes two images and returns one real number.

slides.overview: A worked example of the L1 distance between two images. A formula at the top, then three 4 by 4 grids of pixel values: test image minus training image equals the pixel-wise absolute differences, which add up to 456.
parts: Grid 3, the absolute difference of each pair of pixels.
An arrow labelled add pointing to the total, 456.
slides.relationships: Each cell of grid 3 is the absolute difference of the matching cells in grids 1 and 2. For example the top left cell is 56 minus 10, which is 46. Adding all 16 differences gives the L1 distance of 456.

tables.caption: Pixel-wise absolute value differences (these add up to 456)

slides.overview: A diagram of a linear classifier. An image of a cat goes into a function f of x and W, which outputs 10 class scores. Above it, the equation f of x W equals W x plus b, with the size of every term.
parts: Input: a photo of a cat, an array of 32 by 32 by 3 numbers, 3072 numbers in total.
The function f of x and W, with x shown in blue and W in red.
W, the parameters or weights, feeding into f from below.
slides.relationships: The image x is flattened to a 3072 by 1 column. Multiplying by the 10 by 3072 weight matrix W and adding the 10 by 1 bias b gives a 10 by 1 vector, one score for each class.

math.spoken_context: The same equation with the size of every term.
